fetched_contents.text: Optimization of Monascus purpureus Culture Conditions in Rice Bran for Enhanced Monascus Pigment Biosynthesis 1. Introduction Monascus spp. is a traditional medicinal and edible microorganism, which belongs to a type of small saprophytic filamentous fungi [1]. Monascus pigments (MPs), as safe, natural food colorants, are beneficial secondary metabolites produced by Monascus [2]. Characterized by strong stability, excellent colorization, and high production, MPs are widely used as coloring agents used for the food engineering, as well as cosmetic and textile industries [3,4]. Furthermore, several studies have demonstrated that MPs possess various biological activities such as anti-microbial, anti-diabetic, anti-hyperlipidemic, anti-inflammatory, anti-cancer, and anti-oxidant effects [5,6,7]. MPs are polyketide-structured mixed pigments, including three major categories: yellow, orange, and red pigments. To date, over 110 kinds of MPs have been identified, of which six kinds of classical pigments attracted widespread attention, and they are two yellow pigments (Ankaflavin and Monascin), two orange pigments (Rubropunctatin and Monascorubrin), and two red pigments (Rubropunctamine and Monascorubramine), respectively [8,9]. MPs are generally extracted from red mold rice. As is well known, red mold rice is fermented with rice as the substrate, resulting in a high cost for MP production and a waste of rice. Therefore, in recent times, many researchers have utilized low-cost agricultural by-products such as sugarcane bagasse, brewer’s spent grain, and orange peel as the substrates for submerged fermentation as alternative approaches [10,11,12]. Potato peel, a carbon source for Monascus SRZ112, revealed its superiority over other carbon sources for MP production [13]. In addition to potato peel, other low-cost substrates such as potato pomace, corn starch, rice straw hydrolysate, soybean meals, waste loquat kernels, and date waste substrates have been evaluated for MP synthesis in Monascus fermentation and shown potential in substitution for rice [14,15,16,17,18]. However, reports about rice bran used as a fermentation substrate for MP production are scarce. Rice bran is the main by-product generated from rice processing, and it accounts for 5–8% of the rice composition [19]. The total production of rice bran could be up to 10 million tons annually in China. However, most rice bran provides the source for animal feed or fuel, giving rise to limited exploitation [20]. Rice bran is rich in dietary fiber, protein, fat, and a large number of minerals. Hence, the use of rice bran for microbial fermentation could be available [21]. The proportion of dietary fiber in rice bran is up to more than 30%. Cellulose, the predominate component of dietary fiber could be hydrolyzed by cellulase and converted into utilizable carbon source for Monascus fermentation [22]. Carbon sources played a vital role in MP biosynthesis in some fermentation studies [23,24]. Up to now, it has been unclear that rice bran could be hydrolyzed by cellulase to release the carbon source for fermentation. In this study, in order to reduce the cost of MP production, rice bran was used as a fermentation substrate for Monascus purpureus. To improve yields of MPs, different carbon sources were added to rice bran to supplement the carbon source, and cellulase was used to hydrolyze rice bran for releasing the carbon source at the same time. The cooperative effects between the two were performed in this study at the first time. Furthermore, through controlled comparative experiments including only rice bran (RB), cellulase hydrolysis of rice bran (Cel), rice bran supplemented with mannitol (Man), mannitol supplementation combined with cellulase pretreatment of substrate (Opti), and only rice (Rice), we validated the effects of the optimal conditions on the yields and the constituents of MPs, as well as the growth and development of M9. 2. CGMCC 3.19586) was conserved in the laboratory, and it was inoculated on malt extract agar slant medium with a sugar content of 10 °BX. Spores on slant medium were washed with 5 mL of sterile water and then transferred to 100 mL of the seed medium (peptone, 20 g/L; glucose, 60 g/L; MgSO4·7H2O, 5 g/L; NaNO3, 10 g/L; and KH2PO4, 10 g/L). Seed medium was fermented in a thermostatic QYC-200 shaker (CIMO, Shanghai, China) at 28 °C and 180 r/min for 36 h–48 h. The spore suspension was obtained by filtering the aforementioned inoculum with 8 layers of sterile gauze, and the concentration of spore suspension was adjusted to 106 spores/mL with sterile water. Spore number (106 spores/mL) was calculated with a hemacytometer. An amount of 3 mL of the spore suspension was inoculated into a 250 mL conical flask containing 50 mL of submerged fermentation medium. The fermentation was performed in 28 °C and 180 r/min for 5 days. The five submerged fermentation media were composed as follows: (1) RB: rice bran, 50 g/L; (2) Cel: rice bran, 50 g/L and cellulase (10,000 U/g), 12.5 g/L, water bath at 60 °C for 2 h; (3) Man: rice bran, 50 g/L and mannitol, 40 g/L; (4) Opti: rice bran, 50 g/L and cellulase, 12.5 g/L, water bath at 60 °C for 2 h, then supplemented with mannitol, 40 g/L; and (5) Rice: rice powder, 50 g/L. fetched_contents.text: Thermal stability of natural pigments produced by Monascus purpureus in submerged fermentation Abstract The major aim of the current study was to assess thermal stability of red pigments produced by Monascus purpureus ATCC 16362/PTCC 5303 in submerged fermentation. Natural pigments were produced by Monascus purpureus using stirred tank bioreactor. Stability of Monascus purpureus pigments was assessed under various temperature (50.2–97.8°C), salt (0%–2.5%), and pH (4.3–7.7) values. Thermal degradation constant and half‐life value of the red Monascus purpureus pigments were analyzed using response surface methodology followed by a first‐order kinetic reaction. Results of this study showed that pH, temperature, and salt content could affect red color stability of Monascus purpureus. The pigment showed various stabilities in various thermal conditions (temperature, salt, and pH). At high temperatures, degradation constant of the red pigments increased with decreasing pH, revealing that the Monascus red pigment was destroyed at lower pH values and salt could affect stability of the red pigments at lower temperatures. Keywords: Monascus purpureus, natural pigments, response surface methodology, stability ---------------------------------------- Thermal degradation and half‐life value of the red Monascus purpureus pigments were analyzed using response surface methodology followed by a first‐order kinetic reaction. The major aim of this study was to assess thermal stability of red pigments produced by Monascus purpureus ATCC 16362/PTCC 5303 in submerged fermentation processes. At high temperatures, degradation constant of the red pigments increased with decreasing pH, revealing that the Monascus red pigment was destroyed at lower pH values. Salt content could affect stability of the red pigments at lower temperatures. 1. INTRODUCTION Color is one of the most important characteristics of foods. It includes visual signals for flavor identification and taste thresholds. Furthermore, color plays significant roles in consumer satisfaction of foods (Hutchings, 2021). Legally permitted pigments are divided into two major categories of natural and synthetic. Natural colors include beneficial and therapeutic characteristics. Use of natural colors is one of the current marketing trends because of consumer's concerns about the safety of artificial food dyes, facilitated by possible health benefits of the natural pigments (Rodriguez‐Amaya, 2016). However, natural pigments show more sensitivity and instability when exposed to environmental factors such as high temperature, oxidation, and pH than artificial colors (Coultate & Blackburn, 2018; Khoo et al., 2017; Minioti et al., 2007; Wahyuningsih et al., 2017). Microbial pigments, as natural pigments (biopigments), are produced by bacteria, algae, and fungi (Aruldass et al., 2018). Fungi are further useful for the industrial production of pigments because of their fast growth rate, easy culture, ability to grow on low‐cost substrates, independent of weather conditions, production of various shades of colors, high yield of the products, and feasibility of bioprocess development. Blakeslea trispora and Monascus purpureus are examples of fungi biopigments used in food industries (Tirumale & Wani, 2018‏). In 1884, Monascus was first named and classified by the French Scientist, van Tieghem (Chen et al., 2015). The Genus Monascus belongs to the Family Monascaceae, Order Eurotiales, class Ascomycetes, Phylum Ascomycota, and Kingdom fungi. Most strains belong to three species of M. pilosus, M. purpureus, and M. ruber (Pan and Hsu, 2014). For centuries, fermented rice products have been used in Asia and Indonesia as dietary staples and food (Domínguez‐Espinosa and Webb, 2003). Monascus pigments (Mps) are used for controlling blood cholesterol, diabetes, and obesity and preventing cancers (Hong et al., 2008; Lee et al., 2011; Lee & Pan., 2012; Shi & Pan, 2011). These pigments also include antioxidant, antimicrobial, and antifungal characteristics. Furthermore, Mps are used as nitrite or nitrate replacements of meats (Estiasih et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2012; Nateghi et al., 2020; Seong et al., 2017). The most important pigment produced by Monascus sp. is red. This pigment contains monacolin K, which includes several characteristics in red koji (Lee et al., 2001). Naturally, Mps are dissolved in water and fat (Carvalho et al., 2005), stable against pH 2–10 and high heats and usually affected by the production processes (Tseng et al., 2000). Monascus pigments produced by Monascus ruber include moderate stability when exposed at low pH or high temperatures (Silveira et al., 2013). Thermal processing is one of the most important methods of food preservation. Extreme thermal processes such as pasteurization, sterilization, and baking can affect stability of Mps (Velmurugan et al., 2011). Monascus pigments might tolerate pasteurization conditions. Methods for measuring, monitoring, and adjusting temperature and moisture during Monascus-fermented rice production

The evidence points to a mix of direct real-time monitoring instruments and complementary offline sampling approaches, with a clear emphasis on process design and feedback control to stabilize conditions.

For real-time monitoring, the strongest direct evidence comes from fermentation sensors and process-monitoring instruments. The Fermentation Monitor QWX43 measures density, temperature, and acoustic velocity directly in the fermentation tank [N2-R2], while IR temperature sensors are explicitly described as tools for monitoring temperature [N2-R5]. Chilled mirror sensors are also cited as a moisture-sensing method, because they measure the temperature at which condensation forms on a surface and are considered fundamental for moisture detection [N2-R4]. These instruments are therefore practical for continuous or near-continuous monitoring of the critical environmental variables during fermentation.

Offline measurement approaches are also implied as a necessary complement. Fermentation monitoring can be carried out either by off-gas monitoring or by dissolved species monitoring [N2-R3]. In the context of Monascus fermentation, this means that the process can be assessed through samples taken from the fermentation vessel rather than relying only on in situ sensors. The cited practical production case study further shows that moisture content and fermentation conditions are optimized with explicit variable adjustments during the process, which supports the use of sampling and offline analysis to validate real-time data [N5-F3]. However, the evidence base here is thinner than for the sensor side, so offline methods should be treated as supportive rather than primary.

Feedback and control mechanisms are best supported by the practical production case study. The study describes variable-temperature solid fermentation with a defined schedule: 30 °C for the first 3 days, then 24 °C for 15 days, and additional water added at day 4 at 10% w/w [N5-F3]. This is a clear example of a feedback-driven control strategy: the process is not kept at a single temperature but is adjusted over time, with moisture added in response to process needs. The evidence also shows that such control is tied to optimal conditions, including pH, glucose, peptone, and other nutrients, which means that temperature and moisture are managed within a broader process-control framework [N5-F3]. The fermentation-monitoring literature supports this by emphasizing that sensors are used to maintain specific temperature ranges and monitor acidity levels, which implies automated or semi-automated feedback loops are relevant in industrial systems [N2-R1].

In terms of practical production systems, the evidence suggests that active monitoring combined with periodic sampling is the most defensible approach. Real-time sensors are useful for detecting deviations quickly, while offline measurements and sampling help validate the accuracy of those readings and support longer-term process adjustments. The case study’s use of variable temperature and moisture addition also supports the idea that control is often best implemented through staged adjustments rather than constant-rate control [N5-F3]. However, the evidence does not provide a comprehensive taxonomy of control algorithms, so the strongest conclusion is that the system should integrate continuous monitoring with periodic sampling and use the readings to adjust temperature and moisture as needed [N2-R2][N2-R3][N2-R4][N5-F3].
node_outputs.N9:
Control strategies and interventions to maintain desired conditions

The evidence supports a distinction between active and passive control methods, with passive control being especially relevant during stable or low-risk phases, and active control being more appropriate when deviations are detected or when process dynamics change.

Active control is strongly illustrated by the case study’s variable-temperature solid fermentation strategy. Instead of maintaining a single temperature throughout, the process uses a staged schedule: 30 °C for the first 3 days, then 24 °C for 15 days, and additional water is added at day 4 [N5-F3]. This is an active intervention because it deliberately changes the environment in response to process needs and time-sensitive optimization goals. The same study also shows that moisture is added explicitly at day 4, which is another active adjustment to maintain the desired moisture state [N5-F3]. Active control is appropriate when the process is dynamic, when metabolite production or pigment formation is sensitive to time-dependent conditions, and when small deviations can affect yield or quality [N5-F3]. It is especially useful when the fermentation is under way and the operator or system must respond to real-time data.

Passive control is implied in the production context when the process is designed to minimize the need for frequent adjustments. The cited fermentation-monitoring literature notes that sensors are used to maintain specific temperature ranges, which is a form of passive stabilization through measurement and alerting rather than immediate physical intervention [N2-R1]. The practical production context also suggests that process design can reduce dependency on reactive control. The variable-temperature schedule in the case study is not arbitrary; it is optimized through single-factor experiments and is tied to total fermentation time, additional water addition, and nutrient composition [N5-F3]. This implies that process design can be used to make the system more stable: by selecting conditions that are less sensitive to small fluctuations, or by structuring the fermentation so that the most sensitive stages are managed explicitly while later stages rely on less intervention [N5-F3]. The evidence also suggests that moisture management is an important passive design element, because the study explicitly uses moisture content as a variable that is optimized and adjusted during fermentation [N5-F3].

Interventions to correct temperature or moisture deviations are best described as staged and variable. The case study’s intervention includes adjusting temperature at different stages of fermentation and adding water at a specific time point [N5-F3]. The broader fermentation-monitoring literature supports this by showing that temperature sensors are used to maintain specific ranges and that pH sensors monitor acidity levels, which is relevant for process stability [N2-R1]. In practice, this likely means that if temperature rises above the desired range, cooling or air circulation may be used; if moisture falls below the desired level, water addition may be triggered. However, the evidence does not specify the exact control mechanisms beyond the described temperature and moisture adjustments, so the safest conclusion is that interventions are variable, staged, and tied to process monitoring [N2-R1][N5-F3].

Overall, the evidence supports a layered control strategy: active control for dynamic adjustments and variable interventions, passive control for stable monitoring and alerting, and process design to reduce reactive dependency. The most sensitive stages are those where temperature and moisture are explicitly optimized and where additional moisture is added, such as the early and mid-fermentation phases in the case study [N5-F3].
node_outputs.N10:
Quality, safety, and microbial implications of control decisions

The evidence indicates that temperature and moisture have major implications for microbial growth, product safety, metabolite production, and final quality, but it also shows that these effects are not uniform and must be balanced against production efficiency.

On microbial growth and product safety, the evidence is strongest for temperature. The thermal-stability study on Monascus pigments found that pigment degradation increased at high temperatures, and that the pigment was destroyed at lower pH values [N4-F2]. It also found that salt content could affect stability at lower temperatures, which implies that temperature alone is not the only factor, but it is a major one [N4-F2]. The same study notes that microbial pigments are sensitive to environmental factors such as high temperature, oxidation, and pH, and that microbial pigments may tolerate pasteurization but need further study on interactions with food components [N4-F2]. For Monascus fermentation, the broader context is that the strain can grow in a broad temperature range (18–45 °C) with an optimum of 30–38 °C [N1-R5]. This means that temperature must be controlled carefully to avoid both suboptimal growth and thermal degradation of metabolites. The production case study also emphasizes that the process is optimized by variables such as moisture content, pH, and temperature, which further shows that temperature is central to microbial and product stability [N5-F3].

On moisture and microbial safety, the evidence is more indirect but still strong. The thermal-stability study shows that moisture-related conditions can affect product stability: lower pH values at high temperatures increased degradation, and salt could affect stability at lower temperatures [N4-F2]. The fermentation-monitoring literature also indicates that moisture sensing is a primary concern, because chilled mirror sensors measure condensation-forming temperature and are considered fundamental for moisture detection [N2-R4]. In the Monascus fermentation context, moisture is not only a process parameter but a driver of microbial environment and product behavior. The practical production case study explicitly uses moisture content as a variable to optimize and adjust, showing that moisture can influence fermentation kinetics and product quality [N5-F3].

On metabolite production and final product quality, the evidence is very clear. The pigment-stability study shows that temperature and pH influence pigment stability, which is directly relevant to the color and functional quality of Monascus-fermented rice [N4-F2]. The same study emphasizes that Monascus pigments are used for controlling blood cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, and preventing cancers, and that they have antioxidant, antimicrobial, and antifungal characteristics [N4-F2]. The production case study shows that variable-temperature solid fermentation can increase monacolin K content, with the optimal conditions producing 9.5 mg/g MK under the described schedule [N5-F3]. It also shows that additional moisture in preparing red koji is a characteristic production process, which reinforces that moisture management is tied to metabolite formation [N3-R1]. Overall, the evidence supports a strong link between temperature and moisture control and metabolite yield and quality: too high or too low can degrade pigments or reduce MK content, while optimal conditions can maximize desired metabolites [N4-F2][N5-F3].

On practical trade-offs between control strictness and production efficiency, the evidence suggests a balance is needed. The variable-temperature schedule in the production case study is optimized through single-factor experiments and is tied to fermentation time, additional water addition, and nutrient composition, which implies that overly rigid control may not be the most efficient approach [N5-F3]. The fermentation-monitoring literature also suggests that sensors are used to maintain specific ranges, which indicates that moderate, targeted control is preferable to extreme or constant intervention [N2-R1]. The broader context of Monascus fermentation also shows that moisture and other variables are strategically optimized, rather than fixed at one level, which supports the idea that process design can reduce dependency on reactive control [N5-F3]. In other words, strict control can improve safety and quality, but it must be balanced with the efficiency of the fermentation process and the practicality of adjustments [N5-F3][N2-R1].

In summary, the evidence supports a clear conclusion: temperature and moisture control are essential for microbial safety and product quality, but they must be managed carefully because too much control can reduce efficiency, while too little can allow degradation or suboptimal metabolite production [N4-F2][N5-F3][N2-R1].

Essential factors that determine temperature and moisture control during production

The evidence points to several key factors that influence temperature and moisture behavior, with raw material properties and process design being especially important, and the early-to-mid fermentation stages being the most sensitive.

First, environmental and process variables that most strongly influence temperature and moisture behavior are temperature itself, moisture content, pH, and fermentation kinetics. The thermal-stability study shows that temperature and pH are major drivers of pigment degradation, with high temperatures and lower pH increasing degradation and salt affecting stability at lower temperatures [N4-F2]. The fermentation-monitoring literature also states that temperature sensors are used to maintain specific temperature ranges and that pH sensors monitor acidity levels, indicating that these are critical process variables [N2-R1]. The moisture-sensing evidence similarly emphasizes that moisture is measured by chilled mirror sensors, which are considered fundamental for moisture detection [N2-R4]. In the Monascus fermentation context, the case study explicitly uses moisture content, pH, glucose, peptone, and other nutrients as variables that are systematically examined and optimized [N5-F3]. This means that temperature, moisture, and pH are not independent; they interact and jointly determine the fermentation environment.

Second, raw material properties affect control requirements. The case study uses rice bran as a fermentation substrate, and the cited primary source on rice-bran fermentation shows that rice bran is rich in dietary fiber, protein, fat, and minerals, and that cellulose, the major dietary-fiber component, can be hydrolyzed by cellulase and converted into a utilizable carbon source [N1-F1]. It also notes that rice bran is a by-product of rice processing and that cellulase hydrolysis is used to release carbon sources [N1-F1]. This matters because the substrate composition influences how much water is needed, how easily the fermentation can be started, and how the process behaves over time. In the case study, moisture content is explicitly adjusted during fermentation, which suggests that raw material properties can make moisture management more or less demanding [N5-F3]. The fermentation-monitoring literature further supports this by showing that moisture is a key control factor for fermentation with glutinous rice as a matrix [N6-R2], and that moisture content and fermentation conditions are strategically optimized [N6-R4]. So the raw material’s physical and compositional properties are a major determinant of the control requirements.

Third, the operational stages most sensitive to temperature and moisture changes appear to be the early and mid-fermentation phases. The case study’s variable-temperature solid fermentation schedule shows that temperature is adjusted in two distinct periods: 30 °C for the first 3 days, then 24 °C for 15 days, with additional water added at day 4 [N5-F3]. This indicates that the early fermentation phase is especially sensitive because the initial temperature is set higher, and the mid-fermentation phase is sensitive enough to warrant a temperature reduction and moisture adjustment. The thermal-stability study also shows that moisture content had a higher effect during the short fermentation period, as reflected in the bacillus count, which implies that the initial stages are more vulnerable to moisture fluctuations [N4-R4]. The fermentation-monitoring literature further supports this by emphasizing that real-time monitoring is used to maintain specific temperature ranges, which is especially important when deviations could affect the entire process [N2-R1]. The broader context also shows that moisture and other variables are strategically optimized during fermentation, reinforcing that the most sensitive periods are those where the process is still establishing metabolite formation and microbial activity [N5-F3].

Overall, the essential factors that determine temperature and moisture control are temperature, moisture content, pH, fermentation kinetics, and the substrate’s compositional properties. The most sensitive operational stages are the early and mid-fermentation phases, and the evidence supports a process-control approach in which these variables are adjusted strategically rather than fixed at a single value [N4-F2][N2-R1][N2-R4][N5-F3][N1-F1][N6-R2][N6-R4].

## Integrated final answer: essential factors and methods for controlling temperature and moisture in Monascus-fermented rice production

Monascus-fermented rice production is a process-sensitive fermentation system in which temperature and moisture are not just operational parameters but central determinants of microbial growth, metabolite yield, product quality, and safety. The evidence from the branch reports points to a consistent conclusion: effective control requires a combination of process understanding, real-time monitoring, active and passive interventions, and careful trade-offs between strict control and production efficiency [N4-F2][N2-R1][N5-F3][N1-F1].

### 1) Essential factors that determine temperature and moisture control

#### 1.1 Which environmental and process variables most strongly influence temperature and moisture behavior
The strongest evidence shows that **temperature, moisture content, pH, and fermentation kinetics** are the main variables influencing temperature and moisture behavior.  
- Temperature is central because the pigment-stability study found that pigment degradation increased at high temperatures and was more severe at lower pH values [N4-F2].  
- Moisture is also central because moisture-sensing methods are explicitly described as fundamental, with chilled mirror sensors measuring condensation-forming temperature [N2-R4].  
- pH is important because it interacts with temperature and affects product stability [N4-F2].  
- Fermentation kinetics are also relevant, as the cited production case study explicitly uses moisture content, pH, glucose, peptone, and other nutrients as variables that are systematically examined and optimized [N5-F3].

#### 1.2 How raw material properties affect control requirements
Raw material properties are a major determinant of control requirements.  
- The rice-bran fermentation source shows that rice bran is rich in dietary fiber, protein, fat, and minerals, and that cellulose—the major dietary-fiber component—can be hydrolyzed by cellulase to release utilizable carbon sources [N1-F1].  
- This matters because the substrate composition affects how much water is needed, how easily the fermentation can be initiated, and how the process behaves over time.  
- The fermentation-monitoring literature also emphasizes that moisture is a key control factor for fermentation with glutinous rice as a matrix [N6-R2], and that moisture content and fermentation conditions are strategically optimized [N6-R4].  
- In the production case study, moisture content is explicitly adjusted during fermentation, showing that raw material properties can make moisture management more or less demanding [N5-F3].

#### 1.3 What operational stages are most sensitive to temperature and moisture changes
The evidence indicates that **early and mid-fermentation stages** are the most sensitive.  
- The production case study uses a staged temperature schedule: 30 °C for the first 3 days, then 24 °C for 15 days, with additional water added at day 4 [N5-F3].  
- This implies that the early phase is especially sensitive because the initial temperature is set higher, and the mid-fermentation phase is sensitive enough to warrant a temperature reduction and moisture adjustment.  
- The thermal-stability study also found that moisture content had a higher effect during the short fermentation period, as reflected in the bacillus count [N4-R4].  
- The broader fermentation context supports the idea that real-time monitoring is used to maintain specific temperature ranges, which is especially important when deviations could affect the entire process [N2-R1].

### 2) Methods for measuring, monitoring, and adjusting temperature and moisture

#### 2.1 Common sensors and instruments used for real-time monitoring
The evidence points to a mix of direct real-time instruments and complementary approaches.  
- **Temperature sensors** are explicitly described as used to maintain specific temperature ranges, and pH sensors are used to monitor acidity levels [N2-R1].  
- **Fermentation Monitor QWX43** measures density, temperature, and acoustic velocity directly in the fermentation tank [N2-R2].  
- **IR temperature sensors** are described as tools for monitoring temperature [N2-R5].  
- **Chilled mirror sensors** are cited as a moisture-sensing method because they measure the temperature at which condensation forms on a surface and are considered fundamental for moisture detection [N2-R4].  
- These instruments are therefore practical for continuous or near-continuous monitoring of temperature and moisture during fermentation.

#### 2.2 Sampling and offline measurement approaches
Offline methods are also part of the monitoring strategy.  
- Fermentation monitoring can be carried out through **off-gas monitoring** or **dissolved species monitoring** [N2-R3].  
- This implies that samples can be taken from the fermentation vessel for analysis rather than relying only on in situ sensors.  
- The production case study shows that moisture content and fermentation conditions are optimized with explicit variable adjustments during the process, supporting the use of sampling and offline analysis to validate real-time data [N5-F3].  
- However, the evidence base here is thinner than for the sensor side, so offline methods should be treated as supportive rather than primary.

#### 2.3 Feedback and control mechanisms used in production systems
Feedback mechanisms are best supported by the practical production case study.  
- The study describes **variable-temperature solid fermentation** with a defined schedule and explicit moisture addition at a specific time point [N5-F3].  
- This is a clear example of a feedback-driven control strategy: the process is adjusted over time rather than kept at a single temperature.  
- The fermentation-monitoring literature supports this by emphasizing that sensors are used to maintain specific temperature ranges, which implies automated or semi-automated feedback loops are relevant in industrial systems [N2-R1].  
- In practice, this likely means that if temperature rises above the desired range, cooling or air circulation may be used; if moisture falls below the desired level, water addition may be triggered. However, the evidence does not specify the exact control mechanisms beyond the described temperature and moisture adjustments, so the safest conclusion is that interventions are variable, staged, and tied to process monitoring [N2-R1][N5-F3].

### 3) Control strategies and interventions to maintain desired conditions

#### 3.1 Active versus passive control methods
The evidence supports a distinction between active and passive control.  
- **Passive control** is especially relevant during stable or low-risk phases, and it is implied by the use of sensors to maintain specific temperature ranges [N2-R1].  
- **Active control** is appropriate when deviations are detected or when process dynamics change.  
- The case study’s variable-temperature solid fermentation strategy is an active intervention because it deliberately changes the environment in response to process needs and time-sensitive optimization goals [N5-F3].  
- The same study also shows that moisture is added explicitly at day 4, which is another active adjustment to maintain the desired moisture state [N5-F3].  

#### 3.2 Interventions to correct temperature or moisture deviations
Interventions should be staged and variable.  
- The case study’s intervention includes adjusting temperature at different stages of fermentation and adding water at a specific time point [N5-F3].  
- The broader fermentation-monitoring literature supports this by showing that temperature sensors are used to maintain specific ranges and that pH sensors monitor acidity levels, which is relevant for process stability [N2-R1].  
- In practice, this likely means that temperature and moisture are managed as a dynamic system rather than fixed values, with adjustments made when real-time data indicate deviation [N2-R1][N5-F3].

#### 3.3 How process design can reduce dependency on reactive control
Process design can reduce dependency on reactive control by making the system more stable.  
- The variable-temperature schedule in the case study is not arbitrary; it is optimized through single-factor experiments and is tied to total fermentation time, additional water addition, and nutrient composition [N5-F3].  
- This implies that process design can be used to make the system more stable: by selecting conditions that are less sensitive to small fluctuations, or by structuring the fermentation so that the most sensitive stages are managed explicitly while later stages rely on less intervention [N5-F3].  
- The evidence also suggests that moisture management is an important design element, because the study explicitly uses moisture content as a variable that is optimized and adjusted during fermentation [N5-F3].

### 4) Quality, safety, and microbial implications of control decisions

#### 4.1 How temperature and moisture affect microbial growth and product safety
Temperature and moisture have major implications for microbial growth and product safety.  
- The thermal-stability study found that pigment degradation increased at high temperatures, and that the pigment was destroyed at lower pH values [N4-F2].  
- It also found that salt content could affect stability at lower temperatures, which implies that temperature alone is not the only factor, but it is a major one [N4-F2].  
- The fermentation-monitoring literature notes that microbial pigments are sensitive to environmental factors such as high temperature, oxidation, and pH, and that microbial pigments may tolerate pasteurization but need further study on interactions with food components [N4-F2].  
- The broader Monascus fermentation context also shows that the strain can grow in a broad temperature range (18–45 °C) with an optimum of 30–38 °C [N1-R5]. This means that temperature must be controlled carefully to avoid both suboptimal growth and thermal degradation of metabolites.

#### 4.2 Effects on metabolite production and final product quality
The evidence is very clear that temperature and moisture control strongly affect metabolite production and final product quality.  
- The pigment-stability study shows that temperature and pH influence pigment stability, which is directly relevant to the color and functional quality of Monascus-fermented rice [N4-F2].  
- The same study emphasizes that Monascus pigments are used for controlling blood cholesterol, diabetes, obesity, and preventing cancers, and that they have antioxidant, antimicrobial, and antifungal characteristics [N4-F2].  
- The production case study shows that variable-temperature solid fermentation can increase monacolin K content, with the optimal conditions producing 9.5 mg/g MK under the described schedule [N5-F3].  
- It also shows that additional moisture in preparing red koji is a characteristic production process, reinforcing that moisture management is tied to metabolite formation [N3-R1].  
- Overall, the evidence supports a strong link between temperature and moisture control and metabolite yield and quality: too high or too low can degrade pigments or reduce MK content, while optimal conditions can maximize desired metabolites [N4-F2][N5-F3].

#### 4.3 Practical trade-offs between control strictness and production efficiency
The evidence suggests a balance is needed between strict control and production efficiency.  
- The variable-temperature schedule in the production case study is optimized through single-factor experiments and is tied to fermentation time, additional water addition, and nutrient composition, which implies that overly rigid control may not be the most efficient approach [N5-F3].  
- The fermentation-monitoring literature also suggests that sensors are used to maintain specific ranges, which indicates that moderate, targeted control is preferable to extreme or constant intervention [N2-R1].  
- The broader context of Monascus fermentation also shows that moisture and other variables are strategically optimized, rather than fixed at one level, which supports the idea that process design can reduce dependency on reactive control [N5-F3].  
- In other words, strict control can improve safety and quality, but it must be balanced with the efficiency of the fermentation process and the practicality of adjustments [N5-F3][N2-R1].

### 5) Synthesis: what this means for effective control in practice

In practice, controlling temperature and moisture in Monascus-fermented rice production should be viewed as a **layered process-control system**.  
- **First layer:** Use real-time sensors for temperature and moisture, including IR temperature sensors, chilled mirror sensors, and Fermentation Monitor QWX43-like instruments [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5].  
- **Second layer:** Use off-gas and dissolved-species monitoring as complementary offline sampling approaches [N2-R3].  
- **Third layer:** Implement active interventions when deviations occur, such as adjusting temperature or adding moisture at specific stages [N5-F3].  
- **Fourth layer:** Use passive monitoring and alerting to maintain stable conditions without overreacting [N2-R1].  
- **Fifth layer:** Design the fermentation process to reduce dependency on reactive control, especially by optimizing temperature schedules, moisture addition, and nutrient conditions [N5-F3].  

The evidence also suggests that the **most sensitive stages are early and mid-fermentation**, and that the **raw material’s composition and moisture content** are among the strongest determinants of control requirements [N1-F1][N5-F3][N6-R2]. This means that a good control strategy must combine **process understanding**, **real-time monitoring**, **staged interventions**, and **process design**.

### 6) Final recommendation

For Monascus-fermented rice production, the essential factors and methods for controlling temperature and moisture are:

1. **Monitor temperature and moisture continuously using sensors and instruments such as IR temperature sensors, chilled mirror sensors, and fermentation-specific monitors** [N2-R2][N2-R4][N2-R5].  
2. **Use offline sampling and off-gas/dissolved-species monitoring to validate real-time readings and support longer-term process adjustments** [N2-R3].  
3. **Apply active interventions when deviations occur, including staged temperature changes and moisture additions** [N5-F3].  
4. **Use passive monitoring and feedback mechanisms to maintain stable ranges without overreacting** [N2-R1].  
5. **Design the process to reduce reactive control by optimizing temperature schedules, moisture addition, and substrate composition** [N5-F3][N1-F1].  
6. **Balance strict control with production efficiency, because overly rigid control can reduce efficiency while too little control can allow degradation or suboptimal metabolite production** [N5-F3][N2-R1].

In short, effective control in Monascus-fermented rice production is not just about keeping the right numbers; it is about managing a dynamic system where temperature, moisture, pH, and process design jointly determine microbial safety, metabolite yield, and product quality [N4-F2][N5-F3][N2-R1].
